## Proof

We compute $\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(S^1, \mathbb{Z})$ using the given short exact sequence of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules (abelian groups)

$$0 \to \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{i} \mathbb{R} \xrightarrow{\phi} S^1 \to 0, \qquad \phi(x) = e^{2\pi i x}.$$

Here $i$ is the inclusion and $\phi$ is the universal cover map, so $S^1 \cong \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module.

### Step 1. $\mathbb{R}$ is an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module

As a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, $\mathbb{R}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space (it is uniquely divisible: for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \geq 1$, there is a unique $y = x/n$ with $ny = x$). A divisible abelian group is an injective object in the category of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules (Baer's criterion). Hence

$$\operatorname{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{R}, -) = 0 \quad \text{for all } n \geq 1.$$

### Step 2. Apply $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(-, \mathbb{Z})$ to the short exact sequence

Applying the contravariant functor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(-, \mathbb{Z})$ to $0 \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R} \to S^1 \to 0$ yields the long exact sequence

$$0 \to \operatorname{Hom}(S^1, \mathbb{Z}) \to \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}) \to \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) \to \operatorname{Ext}^1(S^1, \mathbb{Z}) \to \operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}) \to \cdots$$

By Step 1, $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}) = 0$. Also $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) = 0$ since $\mathbb{Z}$ is free (hence projective). The long exact sequence therefore truncates to

$$0 \to \operatorname{Hom}(S^1, \mathbb{Z}) \to \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{i^*} \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) \to \operatorname{Ext}^1(S^1, \mathbb{Z}) \to 0.$$

Consequently

$$\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(S^1, \mathbb{Z}) \cong \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) \big/ \operatorname{im}(i^*).$$

### Step 3. Compute $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z})$

Let $f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z})$. For any $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and any integer $n \geq 1$, unique divisibility of $\mathbb{R}$ gives $x = n \cdot (x/n)$, so

$$f(x) = f\!\left(n \cdot \tfrac{x}{n}\right) = n\, f\!\left(\tfrac{x}{n}\right).$$

Thus $f(x)$ is divisible by every positive integer $n$ in $\mathbb{Z}$. The only integer divisible by all $n \geq 1$ is $0$. Hence $f(x) = 0$ for all $x$, i.e.

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}) = 0.$$

### Step 4. Conclude

Since $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}) = 0$, the map $i^* : \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}) \to \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z})$ is the zero map, so $\operatorname{im}(i^*) = 0$. Also $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ (a homomorphism $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is determined by the image of $1$). Therefore

$$\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(S^1, \mathbb{Z}) \cong \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) \big/ 0 \cong \mathbb{Z}.$$

### Final Answer

$$\boxed{\operatorname{Ext}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}}(S^1, \mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}.}$$

The key points are: (1) $\mathbb{R}$ is a divisible (hence injective) $\mathbb{Z}$-module, killing the higher Ext terms in the long exact sequence; (2) $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}) = 0$ because any homomorphism from a uniquely divisible group into $\mathbb{Z}$ must vanish (its image is divisible in $\mathbb{Z}$, hence trivial); (3) the connecting homomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z} \to \operatorname{Ext}^1(S^1, \mathbb{Z})$ is therefore surjective with zero kernel on the relevant side, giving $\operatorname{Ext}^1(S^1, \mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.
